sources.snippet:
LightRAG introduces a new approach to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems aimed at improving large language models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge sources to provide more accurate and contextually relevant responses. Current RAG systems face limitations such as dependence on flat data representations and insufficient contextual awareness, leading to fragmented answers that miss complex inter-dependencies. LightRAG addresses these issues by incorporating graph structures into text indexing and retrieval processes, enabling more nuanced understanding of entity relationships. The framework features a dual-level retrieval system for both low-level and high-level knowledge discovery, improving retrieval comprehensiveness and efficiency. An incremental update algorithm supports rapid adaptation to new data.

The evaluation of LightRAG across four datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, and Mix) from the UltraDomain benchmark shows significant improvements over existing methods. For example, in the Legal dataset, LightRAG achieves 83.6% win rate in Comprehensiveness against Naive RAG (16.4%) and 84.8% in Overall against RQ-RAG (15.2%). In the Agriculture dataset, it achieves 67.6% win rates in Comprehensiveness, Diversity, and Empowerment against Naive RAG (p. 8). Ablation studies indicate that removing high-level retrieval leads to a performance drop in Comprehensiveness (65.2% vs. 67.6%) and Diversity (72.8% vs. 76.4%), and removing low-level retrieval results in a drop in Comprehensiveness (64.0% vs. 67.6%) and Empowerment (65.2% vs. 67.6%) (p. 9).

LightRAG is more efficient than GraphRAG in terms of token and API usage. During retrieval, LightRAG uses fewer than 100 tokens and one API call, while GraphRAG consumes 610,000 tokens and hundreds of API calls. During incremental updates, LightRAG integrates new data without full reconstruction, whereas GraphRAG requires rebuilding 1,399 communities, leading to a token cost of around 1,399 × 2 × 5,000 (p. 10). The system is open-source and available at https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG.

LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation introduces a new approach to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, aiming to enhance large language models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge sources to provide more accurate and contextually relevant responses (p. 1). Current RAG systems face limitations such as dependence on flat data representations and insufficient contextual awareness, leading to fragmented answers that miss complex inter-dependencies (p. 1). The proposed LightRAG addresses these issues by incorporating graph structures into text indexing and retrieval processes (p. 1). This framework features a dual-level retrieval system for comprehensive information retrieval from both low-level and high-level knowledge discovery (p. 1). The combination of graph structures with vector representations enables efficient retrieval of related entities and relationships, improving response times while maintaining contextual relevance (p. 1). An incremental update algorithm ensures timely integration of new data, making the system effective in dynamic environments (p. 1). Experimental validation shows significant improvements in retrieval accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods (p. 1). LightRAG is open-source and available at https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG (p. 1).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems aim to improve large language models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge sources, such as domain-specific information and up-to-date data (p. 1). Chunking is a key technique used to break down large text corpora into smaller segments, enhancing retrieval accuracy (p. 1). However, current RAG systems face limitations, including the use of flat data representations that hinder the understanding of complex entity relationships and a lack of contextual awareness, leading to fragmented responses (p. 1). For example, a query about how electric vehicles influence urban air quality and public transportation may yield separate documents but fail to provide a cohesive explanation of the interdependencies (p. 1).

To address these limitations, the authors propose incorporating graph structures into text indexing and information retrieval (p. 2). Graphs effectively represent entity interdependencies, enabling more nuanced understanding and coherent responses (p. 2). The proposed system, LightRAG, integrates a dual-level retrieval framework with graph-enhanced text indexing. Low-level retrieval focuses on precise entity relationships, while high-level retrieval captures broader topics (p. 2). This approach improves retrieval comprehensiveness and efficiency while supporting rapid adaptation to new data through an incremental update algorithm (p. 2). The system was evaluated through extensive experiments focusing on retrieval accuracy, model ablation, response efficiency, and adaptability, showing significant improvements over baseline methods (p. 2).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines user queries with relevant documents from an external knowledge database using two components: the Retrieval Component and the Generation Component (p. 2). The retrieval component identifies and retrieves relevant data based on the query, while the generation component uses this information to generate coherent responses (p. 2). Formally, the RAG framework M is defined as $ M = (G, R = (\phi, \psi)) $, where G is the generation module, R is the retrieval module, q is the input query, and D is the external database (p. 2). The retrieval module R includes two key functionalities: i) the Data Indexer $ \phi(\cdot) $, which builds a specific data structure $ \hat{D} $ based on D, and ii) the Data Retriever $ \psi(\cdot) $, which retrieves relevant documents by comparing the query to the indexed data (p. 3). The generative model G then uses the retrieved documents and the query to produce responses (p. 3). This work emphasizes three key aspects for an effective RAG system: Comprehensive Information Retrieval, which requires the indexing function $ \phi(\cdot) $ to extract global information for better query answering (p. 3); Efficient and Low-Cost Retrieval, requiring $ \hat{D} $ to enable fast and cost-effective retrieval for high query volumes (p. 3); and Fast Adaptation to Data Changes, ensuring the system can quickly incorporate new information to stay current (p. 3).

LightRAG enhances retrieval systems by segmenting documents into manageable pieces and using LLMs to extract entities and relationships, forming a knowledge graph (page 3). This graph is created through three steps: entity and relationship extraction using R(·), key-value pair generation via P(·), and deduplication using D(·) to optimize graph operations (page 3). The graph-based indexing allows for efficient multi-hop subgraph extraction and improved retrieval performance over embedding matching and chunk traversal methods (page 4). LightRAG supports fast adaptation to incremental knowledge bases by updating the graph with new documents without reprocessing the entire dataset (page 4). The dual-level retrieval paradigm addresses specific and abstract queries, using low-level and high-level retrieval strategies to handle detailed and conceptual questions (page 4). LightRAG integrates graph structures with vector representations to streamline search and enhance result relevance through keyword matching and high-order relatedness (page 5). Retrieved information is used by an LLM to generate answers, combining entity and relation values for context-aware responses (page 5). Complexity analysis shows that the graph-based indexing phase involves calling the LLM for each chunk size, with no additional overhead (page 5). The retrieval phase uses vector-based search to retrieve entities and relationships, reducing overhead compared to community-based traversal methods in GraphRAG (page 5).

The evaluation section of the document assesses the LightRAG framework against existing RAG methods across four datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, and Mix) from the UltraDomain benchmark. Each dataset contains between 600,000 and 5,000,000 tokens. Evaluation is based on 125 questions generated by an LLM for each dataset, covering diverse domains and user-task combinations. The study compares LightRAG with four baselines: Naive RAG, RQ-RAG, HyDE, and GraphRAG. Evaluation dimensions include Comprehensiveness, Diversity, Empowerment, and Overall, using GPT-4o-mini to rank responses.

Results in Table 1 show that LightRAG outperforms all baselines in most cases. For example, in the Legal dataset, LightRAG achieves 83.6% win rate in Comprehensiveness against Naive RAG (16.4%) and 84.8% in Overall against RQ-RAG (15.2%). In the Agriculture dataset, LightRAG achieves 67.6% win rates in Comprehensiveness, Diversity, and Empowerment against Naive RAG. GraphRAG performs better than LightRAG in some cases, particularly in the Legal dataset (48.4% vs. 51.6% in Comprehensiveness), but LightRAG still shows a consistent advantage in most datasets (6-10).

Ablation studies in Table 2 reveal the effectiveness of LightRAG’s dual-level retrieval paradigm. Removing high-level retrieval (LightRAG) leads to a performance drop in Comprehensiveness (65.2% vs. 67.6%) and Diversity (72.8% vs. 76.4%). Removing low-level retrieval (LightRAG) results in a drop in Comprehensiveness (64.0% vs. 67.6%) and Empowerment (65.2% vs. 67.6%). The hybrid mode of LightRAG combines both retrieval levels and performs best. Additionally, the variant that omits the use of original text (-Origin) performs comparably or better than the standard version, especially in Agriculture (75.2% vs. 67.6%).

A case study in Table 3 compares LightRAG and GraphRAG responses to a machine learning question. LightRAG is ranked superior in all evaluation dimensions, providing a broader range of metrics and more nuanced explanations. The LLM judge identifies LightRAG as the winner in Comprehensiveness, Diversity, Empowerment, and Overall.

Cost analysis in Figure 2 and Table 2 highlights LightRAG’s efficiency. In the retrieval phase, LightRAG uses fewer than 100 tokens and one API call, while GraphRAG consumes 610,000 tokens and hundreds of API calls. During incremental updates, LightRAG integrates new data without full reconstruction, whereas GraphRAG requires rebuilding 1,399 communities, leading to a token cost of around 1,399 × 2 × 5,000. LightRAG’s approach is significantly more cost-effective and adaptable to dynamic data changes (p. 10).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance LLM inputs by retrieving relevant information from external sources, improving factual and domain-specific responses (p. 10). Current RAG approaches embed queries in a vector space to find the nearest context vectors but often rely on fragmented text chunks and top-k retrieval, limiting comprehensive global information (p. 10). Recent studies have explored using graph structures for knowledge representation, but these methods often lack the capability for dynamic updates and expansions, making it difficult to incorporate new information effectively (p. 10). The proposed model, LightRAG, addresses these challenges by enabling the RAG system to adapt to new information, ensuring timeliness and accuracy (p. 10). Existing methods also rely on inefficient brute-force searches for each generated community, which LightRAG overcomes through a dual-level retrieval paradigm, enhancing retrieval efficiency and response speed (p. 10). Graphs are a powerful framework for representing complex relationships, and researchers have focused on enhancing LLMs' ability to interpret graph-structured data (p. 10). This work is divided into three categories: GNNs as Prefix, where GNNs generate structure-aware tokens for LLMs (e.g., GraphGPT, LLaGA) (p. 10); LLMs as Prefix, where LLMs process graph data to refine GNN training (e.g., GALM, OFA) (p. 10); and LLMs-Graphs Integration, focusing on seamless interaction between LLMs and graph data using fusion training, GNN alignment, and LLM-based agents (p. 10).

This work introduces an advancement in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) through the integration of a graph-based indexing approach that enhances both efficiency and comprehension in information retrieval (p. 10). LightRAG utilizes a comprehensive knowledge graph to facilitate rapid and relevant document retrieval, enabling a deeper understanding of complex queries (p. 10). Its dual-level retrieval paradigm allows for the extraction of both specific and abstract information, catering to diverse user needs (p. 10). Furthermore, LightRAG’s seamless incremental update capability ensures that the system remains current and responsive to new information, thereby maintaining its effectiveness over time (p. 10). Overall, LightRAG excels in both efficiency and effectiveness, significantly improving the speed and quality of information retrieval and generation while reducing costs for LLM inference (p. 10).

The appendix of the document provides detailed methodologies and experimental settings used in the LightRAG framework. It describes the steps for extracting entities and relationships from documents using large language models (LLMs), including the prompt templates and configurations for LLM operations. The section also outlines evaluation criteria for assessing LightRAG's performance against baselines (p. 13).

Table 4 presents statistical information for four datasets: Agriculture (12 documents, 2,017,886 tokens), CS (10 documents, 2,306,535 tokens), Legal (94 documents, 5,081,069 tokens), and Mix (61 documents, 619,009 tokens) (p. 13).

The document illustrates the retrieve-and-generate process in Figure 3, where the LLM extracts keywords to guide dual-level retrieval on a knowledge graph, organizing retrieved information into entities, relationships, and text chunks to generate a comprehensive answer to a query (p. 14).

Prompts for graph generation (Figure 4) focus on extracting entity-relationship information, while prompts for query generation (Figure 5) define user roles and tasks for generating dataset-based queries (p. 14). Prompts for keyword extraction (Figure 6) distinguish between high-level and low-level keywords, returning them in JSON format (p. 15). The RAG evaluation prompt (Figure 7) compares answers based on Comprehensiveness, Diversity, and Empowerment (p. 15).

Table 5 compares LightRAG and NaiveRAG in answering a question about Indigenous perspectives in corporate mergers. LightRAG provides a more comprehensive, diverse, and empowering answer, emphasizing cultural significance, collaboration, and legal frameworks, while NaiveRAG lacks depth in analyzing the various dimensions of Indigenous ownership and collaboration (p. 16). The evaluation, structured in JSON, determines LightRAG as the overall winner (p. 16).

In this section, we analyze the complexity of our proposed LightRAG framework, which can be
divided into two main parts. The first part is the graph-based Index phase. During this phase, we use
the large language model (LLM) to extract entities and relationships from each chunk of text. As
a result, the LLM needs to be called total tokenschunk size times. Importantly, there is no additional overheadinvolved in this process, making our approach highly efficient in managing updates to new text.
The second part of the process involves the graph-based retrieval phase. For each query, we first
utilize the large language model (LLM) to generate relevant keywords. Similar to current Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) systems Gao et al. (2023; 2022); Chan et al. (2024), our retrieval
mechanism relies on vector-based search. However, instead of retrieving chunks as in conventional
RAG, we concentrate on retrieving entities and relationships. This approach markedly reduces
retrieval overhead compared to the community-based traversal method used in GraphRAG.

What specific advantages does LightRAG demonstrate through case examples in various scenarios? •
(RQ4): What are the costs associated with LightRAG, as well as its adaptability to data changes?

ABSTRACT
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models
(LLMs) by integrating external knowledge sources, enabling more accurate and
contextually relevant responses tailored to user needs. However, existing RAG
systems have significant limitations, including reliance on flat data representa-
tions and inadequate contextual awareness, which can lead to fragmented answers
that fail to capture complex inter-dependencies. To address these challenges, we
propose LightRAG, which incorporates graph structures into text indexing and
retrieval processes. This innovative framework employs a dual-level retrieval sys-
tem that enhances comprehensive information retrieval from both low-level and
high-level knowledge discovery. Additionally, the integration of graph structures
with vector representations facilitates efficient retrieval of related entities and their
relationships, significantly improving response times while maintaining contextual
relevance. This capability is further enhanced by an incremental update algorithm
that ensures the timely integration of new data, allowing the system to remain
effective and responsive in rapidly changing data environments. Extensive experi-
mental validation demonstrates considerable improvements in retrieval accuracy
and efficiency compared to existing approaches. We have made our LightRAG
open-source and available at the link: https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG.

Current RAG systems face limitations such as flat data representations and inadequate contextual awareness, leading to fragmented responses [1]. LightRAG addresses these issues by incorporating graph structures into text indexing and retrieval processes, enabling a more nuanced understanding of entity relationships [1]. The framework features a dual-level retrieval system for both low-level and high-level knowledge discovery, improving retrieval comprehensiveness and efficiency [1]. An incremental update algorithm ensures the system can adapt to new data efficiently [1].

LightRAG was evaluated across four datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, and Mix) from the UltraDomain benchmark, showing significant improvements over existing methods [1]. For example, in the Legal dataset, LightRAG achieved an 83.6% win rate in Comprehensiveness against Naive RAG (16.4%) and an 84.8% win rate in Overall against RQ-RAG (15.2%) [1]. In the Agriculture dataset, it achieved 67.6% win rates in Comprehensiveness, Diversity, and Empowerment against Naive RAG [1]. Ablation studies showed that removing high-level retrieval led to performance drops in Comprehensiveness (65.2% vs. 67.6%) and Diversity (72.8% vs. 76.4%), while removing low-level retrieval affected Comprehensiveness (64.0% vs. 67.6%) and Empowerment (65.2% vs. 67.6%) [1]. LightRAG is more efficient than GraphRAG in terms of token and API usage, using fewer than 100 tokens and one API call during retrieval, compared to GraphRAG's 610,000 tokens and hundreds of API calls [1]. The system is open-source and available at https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG [1].
